title: Weaver, shoemaker, barber, king
hook: the Bhagats' trades read like a street; that's the point

segments.voice: Yesterday, greed: Farid's words kept whole, and Guru Amar Das answering beside them. Today, a walk down the Bhagats' street.

A clatter from a loom in a doorway. Next door, someone bent over a shoe, stitching leather. Further on, a barber with a razor and a customer half-shaved. A farmer coming in from the fields with mud on his feet. And at the end of the road, a palace. Walk the names of the Bhagats in the Guru Granth Sahib and that's the street you're walking down: weaver, shoemaker, barber, king.
screen: `A LOOM IN A DOORWAY.` → `LEATHER, A RAZOR, A MUDDY FARMER.` → `A PALACE AT THE END OF THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Some of these trades come from the Bhagats' own mouths. Kabir calls himself a weaver in his hymns, and works the loom into his songs. Namdev says he was born in the house of a calico printer. Ravidas says his family carried the dead cattle, work the caste order of his day looked down on. Others come from tradition: Sain the barber, Dhanna the farmer, Pipa the king who gave up his throne. Side by side, they don't read like a list of holy men from one class. They read like a street. That's the point. Ravidas's own hymns show a town that ranked people by birth, where a leather-worker's touch was counted as polluting. The Granth answers by putting the weaver's song, the leather-worker's song and the king's song on the same pages, in the same raags, under the same honor. The barber's hymn is sung with the same reverence as the king's. Guru Nanak says it in his own words in Raag Asa, in paraphrase: recognize the light in everyone, and don't ask about caste; in the world beyond, there is no caste. So the mix of trades isn't decoration. It's the teaching, made visible. You can't hold the Guru Granth Sahib in your hands and keep the street out of it. And it runs both ways: the king isn't shut out either. Pipa's place there is as a devotee, beside the others, not above them.
screen: `IN THEIR OWN WORDS: LOOM, PRINT, CATTLE.` · `IN TRADITION: BARBER, FARMER, KING.` · `DON'T ASK ABOUT CASTE.` · `THE MIX IS THE TEACHING.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE STREET.`

segments.voice: Walk your own street in your mind: whoever drives the bus, stacks the shelves, cuts hair, answers the phone, runs the office. Picture their faces as clearly as you can, each one a name on the same page. If you pray, let Waheguru go with each breath out.
Weaver. Kabir's own word for himself, at the head of a street of Bhagats: weaver, printer, leather worker, barber, farmer, king.
Your line: the whole street. Loom, razor, field and palace, on the same pages. Day seven hundred ninety-six, done.

howItsDone: Sikhs point to the Bhagats' different trades and castes as part of the Guru Granth Sahib's teaching that birth sets no limit on devotion, and the langar, where all sit together, puts the same teaching into practice.

chat.says: Why does the Guru Granth Sahib include a weaver, a barber and a king?
options: The mix is the teaching: don't ask about caste; every devotee shares the same pages.
It ranks them by trade, so the king's hymns are honored above the rest.
They were all Brahmins by birth who took up trades later in life.
chat.meaning: Kabir, Namdev and Ravidas name their trades; tradition adds barber, farmer and king. The Granth sets all their songs side by side under the same honor.

Kabir.meaning: the weaver-poet whose hymns are in the Granth

Namdev.meaning: a Bhagat born in a calico printer's house

Ravidas.meaning: a Bhagat from a family of leather-workers

Pipa.meaning: a king, tradition says, who became a devotee

Asa.meaning: a raag, or musical mode, of the Granth

notes: Kabir calling himself a weaver (julaha) and Namdev saying he was born in a calico printer's (chhipa) house: from their hymns; a Keeper may wish to add Ang references.

Ravidas, 'my family carried the dead cattle' (meri jaat kutband dhaalaa dhor dhovantaa): cited as Malar, Ang 1293; confirm Ang. 'Work the caste order of his day looked down on' reflects the caste order of the time; confirm wording.
Sain the barber, Dhanna the farmer, Pipa the king who gave up his throne: attributed to tradition.
'The Gurus' own hymns say what counts before God is not caste but devotion and deeds': general; a Keeper may wish to cite a line.

Editor pass: replaced the unsourced historical sweep ('birth decided who could approach God, read the texts, stand near the temple') with what Ravidas's cited hymns show, replaced the general 'the Gurus' hymns say' with a paraphrase of Guru Nanak's Asa line (jaanahu jot na poochhahu jaatee, aagai jaat na he, Ang 349: confirm Ang) and added it to sources; reworked the practice so it doesn't repeat day 778's unseen-worker angle; varied the hook ending and practice opener.
